section_summary: The section ends a survey of Japanese magazine commentary on labor and includes a Political Adviser’s despatch enclosing a glossary of American labor terms for use in Japan. A second despatch and report record an October 1947 discussion among occupation officials and Japanese labor and political leaders. The final despatch introduces a long report on press and radio unions, their disputes over editorial control, the failed October 1946 strike, and subsequent labor-management relations; that report continues beyond page 245.

subfiles.title: Survey of Japanese magazine views on labor
subfiles.about: Japanese magazine writers assess labor disputes, union maturity, education, management councils, and labor law.
subfiles.summary: The concluding pages contrast hopes for democratic unions with concerns about premature strikes, weak organization, and limited worker education. Writers discuss management councils, labor legislation, the constitutional standard of living, and the need for cooperation in economic recovery. A final source list identifies magazines, circulation figures, and authors.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of English-Japanese Glossary of Labor Terms
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of a standardized American labor terminology list for occupation personnel and Japanese unions.
subfiles.summary: Forwards five copies of a labor terms glossary.

subfiles.title: Word List of American Labor Terminology
subfiles.from: James S. Killen, Chief, Labor Division
subfiles.about: Introduces and supplies English labor terms with Hepburn romanizations and Japanese equivalents.
subfiles.summary: The Labor Division explains that standardized terminology should help field officers, interpreters, and Japanese unions discuss American labor concepts. It invites corrections to the preliminary list. The following pages provide an alphabetic English–Hepburn–Japanese glossary covering union organization, bargaining, wages, strikes, workplace rules, and related terms.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of a Report Concerning a Discussion of Labor Problems at an Asiatic Society Study Group Meeting
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Introduces the enclosed account of a discussion on Japanese labor’s position and the use of strikes.
subfiles.summary: Sebald identifies the principal participants and highlights disputes over strikes, mediation, teachers’ unions, and possible October labor action.

subfiles.title: Japanese Labor’s Present Position
subfiles.about: Records a discussion among occupation officials and Japanese political and labor leaders about unions, strikes, wages, and economic recovery.
subfiles.summary: Kan describes Sambetsu’s membership, mistakes, and economic demands; Stanchfield questions when strikes are justified in Japan’s weak economy. Yamada, Kan, Suzuki, and Kato debate political strikes, collective bargaining, production, wages, and labor relations committees. Other questions address limits on the right to strike, union overlap, teachers’ unions, and management councils.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of a Report Concerning the Relationship of Labor Organizations to the Press and Radio
subfiles.about: Forwards a report on press and radio unions and their relationship with editorial management.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the September report under separate cover.

subfiles.title: Some Aspects of Labor Organization in the Press and Radio in Postwar Japan
subfiles.from: Information Media Research, Civil Information and Education Section
subfiles.about: Examines press and radio unionization, editorial independence, major disputes, and developing labor-management practices after Japan’s surrender.
subfiles.summary: The report argues that employee unions helped reorganize major newspapers after surrender but, in some cases, claimed editorial powers that conflicted with management responsibility for a free press. It traces disputes at the Asahi, Mainichi, Yomiuri, Hokkaido Shimbun, and the Broadcasting Corporation of Japan, culminating in the failed October 1946 press and radio strike. Later chapters describe contracts, management councils, wage negotiations, and a movement away from militant union leadership at several newspapers. The report continues after page 245.
